The Wonga pigeon Ocyphaps lophotes is a common resident of eastern Australian woodlands where detailed physiological work remains scarce. Recent respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions have provided a reliable estimate of the species' energetic ceiling. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for this bird was 195.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 195.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], measured at an ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This value, obtained from post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, aligns well with predictions for a moderately sized columbid and suggests that the Wonga pigeon possesses a metabolic capacity suited to its sedentary, frugivorous lifestyle. Further comparative work across the Columbidae would help determine whether this rate is typical for the genus or reflects specific adaptations to the relatively stable microclimates of sclerophyll forests.

Reproductive output in the Wonga pigeon is modest but consistent with the pattern seen in many terrestrial pigeons. Females produce exactly 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], and field observations confirm that they raise a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive schedule is likely constrained by the extended period of parental care required by the altricial nestlings and the seasonal availability of fruits and seeds. The species does not exhibit the multiple-brooding strategy common among many smaller columbids, instead investing considerable time and energy into each nesting attempt. The nest itself is a fragile platform of twigs placed in dense shrubbery, which females construct while the male gathers materials. Clutch size appears invariant across the species' range, with no reports of annual double-brooding even in regions with extended growing seasons.

Development during incubation and the early nestling period proceeds rapidly when temperatures are optimal. Eggs maintained at a stable incubation temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] hatch after approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days], a relatively short duration for a bird of this adult body size. The literature reports a range of 18 to 20 days across different studies, but the value from controlled incubation is well established. Newly hatched chicks are altricial, weighing just 9.5 grams [Wwb = 9.5 grams], and they depend entirely on parental provisioning of crop milk and soft fruits. This modest birth mass represents a small fraction of the ultimate adult weight, highlighting the substantial growth that must occur during the nestling and fledgling phases. The precise thermal requirements for successful development underscore the importance of the female's attentive brooding behavior, which maintains the nest microclimate even during cooler periods.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is apparent in adult Wonga pigeons, with males reaching a larger asymptotic mass. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 199.4 grams [Wwi = 199.4 grams], while males are heavier at an ultimate wet weight of 210 grams [Wwi = 210 grams]. This difference of approximately 10 grams is modest but consistent across populations and likely reflects sexual selection on male body size, perhaps related to competitive interactions over territories or access to mates. The adult mass is attained gradually after fledging, as young birds continue to refine their foraging skills and accumulate reserves. The species maintains a relatively stable body condition throughout the year in productive habitats, though individuals in drier regions may experience seasonal fluctuations tied to fruit abundance. These mass estimates were derived from large series of museum specimens measured in the austral summer.

Under the warm thermal conditions typical of the active period for this species, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the developmental schedule following hatching unfolds predictably. Young Wonga pigeons achieve fledging, defined as the age at which sustained flight is first possible, after 24 days [tx = 24 days] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Shortly thereafter, the onset of puberty, marking the completion of gonadal maturation, occurs at 80 days [tp = 80 days] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. First reproduction, however, is substantially delayed, with individuals typically producing their first brood at 693.5 days since birth [tR = 693.5 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, also under these thermal conditions, is 6168.5 days [am = 6168.5 days], a longevity that permits several breeding seasons and suggests a relatively slow life-history pace compared to many small passerines at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. These timing estimates, derived from captive colony data, may vary in wild populations depending on resource availability and predation pressure.
